name: moon

text: The moon was a cosmological object of importance to the Celts. Its changing phases and its ties to the tides drew their notice. The Celts first divided the year by the moons. Pliny, the Roman author, said the new moon began each month, as night began each day. The Celts held festivals at moonrise. May Eve, the evening before Beltane, is one such night. Hallowe'en, the evening before Samhain, is another. Some scholars hold that the moon meant most to farmers. Its waxing and waning was thought to guide plant growth, as it does the tides. Mistletoe and other magical plants were gathered under a waning moon. In the Scottish Highlands sowing was done under a waxing moon, so that seeds would swell as the moon swelled. Strabo, the Roman author, recorded night-long dancing at the full moon. That dancing went on at stone circles in the Scottish Highlands through the 18th century. In the 19th century people still bowed to the new moon in the insular Celtic lands. In Cornwall people only nodded and touched their money for luck. A full moon drew Irish folk to crossroads to dance. Priestly opposition nearly ended that custom, but it revived around Ennis, County Clare, and other rural regions.

okr.objective: Document the moon and its place in Celtic year and ritual.
